subject: Surge activation timelines and streaming handshake
messages:
From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwoodinference.com>
To: Sarah Mills <sarah@fastpay.com>
Cc: karthik.iyer@redwoodinference.com, laura.bennett@redwoodinference.com
Date: Tue, 14 Mar 2028 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Recap + proposed test plan: surge activation timelines and streaming handshake

Hi Sarah —

Thanks again for taking time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have a single canonical plan going into the technical test. I captured the requirements we discussed and a pragmatic Redwood approach to validate SLOs under surge conditions.

What you asked for (requirements we captured)
- Streaming: token-by-token streaming for responses, client-visible chunks within 80ms per token for typical payloads (p50 < 40ms, p95 < 120ms for 512-token responses).
- Throughput: sustain 120 requests/sec for 1 minute during peak windows, bursting to 350 req/sec for up to 60s.
- Concurrency: support 240 concurrent active streams without per-request queuing degrading below the p95 latency target.
- Scale-up: ability to recover target concurrency within 90s from baseline traffic after a cold spike (you asked: can this be < 2s? we'll explain below).

Redwood proposal (what we'll validate in the test)
1) Test window: 1-hour run. 20m baseline -> 20m spike profile (gradual then sudden) -> 20m steady-state recovery.
2) Test traffic: we will use your sample payloads (please confirm the test dataset in the attached test-data-sample.json).
3) Measurement: we will report per-token latency histograms, connection/keepalive stats, queue depth over time, and tail latencies per host.
4) Activation strategy we'll exercise: warm pool + incremental activation + soft queueing. We aim to show warm-pool hit ratio, scale-up latency, and how streaming sessions are prioritized versus new connections.
5) Success criteria (pass/fail gating): p95 token latency <= 120ms during sustained 120 rps; sustained 350 rps burst should produce < 5% dropped streams and tail recovery within 120s.

Immediate asks for the test
- Permission to run the load test in your staging environment on Tue 21 Mar 2028 10:00–11:00 PT.
- Confirm the sample dataset (attached). If you prefer, we can use an anonymized subset of production traces.
- If you have any firewall/IP allowlist constraints please send the IPs or a ticket to your networking team; we can also run the test from our dedicated test pool if that is easier.

Attachments: MAP draft (FP-MAP-draft.pdf) with milestones and responsibilities; test sample (test-data-sample.json).

Karthik and Laura are on copy — Karthik will own runtime configuration and will post the priming/priming-config we intend to use. Laura can coordinate scheduling and outcome tracking in HubSpot.

Next steps
- Sarah: confirm dataset and accept the 21 Mar time (or propose alternate).
- Redwood: prep priming config and a short run to verify warm-pool sizing prior to the larger run.

Thanks — looking forward.

--
Jonas Weber
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
jonas.weber@redwoodinference.com

From: Sarah Mills <sarah@fastpay.com>

Subject: Re: Recap + proposed test plan: surge activation timelines and streaming handshake

Jonas — thanks for the clear summary. A few clarifying items so we can sign off on the test plan: 

1) Scale-up SLA: you mentioned 90s to recover target concurrency. Can you give us the breakdown — e.g., how much of that is kernel/container startup vs. redistributing existing KV caches vs. model parameter loading? We need this to make an internal commitment for our ops runbooks.

2) Warm pool sizing: what is Redwood’s recommended minimum pre-warmed capacity for our profile (we currently see short spikes to 300 concurrent sessions for <60s twice daily)? If the warm pool is 20% of expected peak, will you still meet the p95 target or do we need 40%?

3) Streaming connection behavior: in the worst-case burst scenario, do existing streaming sessions stay live (i.e., continue to receive tokens) while new sessions queue, or do you reallocate CPU/GPU and cause transient stalls? We need to ensure merchant-facing flows don’t experience visible stalls.

4) If you can provide a short note on what metrics you’ll deliver in the post-test report that would be helpful (we want to attach them to our operational runbook).

We can tentatively hold Tues 21 Mar 10:00–11:00 PT. I’ll try to get our SRE (on cc) to clear the allowlist if you give IPs.

Thanks,
Sarah
Sr. Product Ops, FastPay
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodinference.com>
To: Sarah Mills <sarah@fastpay.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: laura.bennett@redwoodinference.com
Date: Wed, 15 Mar 2028 08:26:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Recap + proposed test plan: surge activation timelines and streaming handshake

Sarah — hi, Karthik from Redwood infra. Short technical reply with measured expectations and what we’ll demonstrate during the run.

High-level breakdown for scale-up latency (typical numbers from our dedicated-test fleet):
- Kernel/container warm-up (if a fresh instance is required): 4–10s (depends on instance type and preloaded kernels).
- Model KV/cache population for streaming (when activating additional model workers): 2–40s depending on whether we can hydrate from a nearby warm replica; typical incremental worker comes up with a lightweight cache and then backfills hot keys in ~20s for a 512-token working set.
- Runtime routing and connection handoff: <2s for routing table updates; actual client connections remain bound to their original worker until instructing a graceful handoff.

Important operational detail: we do not terminate in-flight streaming sessions to activate capacity. Existing sessions continue on the host they were established on; we prioritize in-flight streams over the admission of new sessions for the first 30–60s of a surge. New sessions are placed in a short admission queue (soft FIFO) that allows the connection handshake to complete but delays initial token emission until we can assign a worker. That behavior prevents visible stalls for established merchant-facing flows.

Warm-pool guidance for your profile (300 concurrent spikes):
- Conservative: pre-warm 40% of expected peak (120 active workers) to hit p95 targets with <5% queueing during sudden spikes.
- Aggressive cost-optimized: 20% warm pool with an aggressive priming policy where we keep a small hot key subset replicated across warm instances; this can meet p95 under many scenarios but will increase the chance of short admission queueing during the largest bursts.

How we’ll measure and report (what you’ll get after the run):
- Per-token latency histograms (p50/p95/p99) aggregated by response length buckets (<=64, <=256, <=512 tokens).
- Connection-level traces showing start time, first-token latency, total tokens emitted, and whether the session was served by warm or newly activated worker.
- Queue depth over time and admission queue wait-time percentiles.
- Warm-pool hit ratio and per-host load curves.
- Annotation of any retries or dropped streams (we’ll attach raw event logs for any failures).

Attachments: I’ve attached the last comparable run log (scale-run-20280305.log) and the priming policy we intend to use (priming-config.yaml). The priming config keeps hot tokens for your top-20 prompt templates replicated across the warm pool.

Recommendation for the test: run a short priming pass 30 minutes before the main 1-hour window to maximize warm-pool hit ratio. We’ll also run a small 5–10 minute smoke test 1 hour before to verify network/allowlist.

If you want, during the run I can stream a live dashboard link to your SRE team so you can watch queue depth and token-level latencies in near real time.

--
Karthik Iyer
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
karthik.iyer@redwoodinference.com
